text: Before you can understand what makes a qubit strange, you need to be precise about what a classical bit actually is, not the hand-wavy version, the formal one. This lesson builds that foundation so the contrast coming up really lands.

A classical bit is a physical system with exactly two stable, distinguishable states, labeled 0 and 1 purely by convention — a voltage level, a magnetic domain, a punched hole. Three properties define how it behaves. Determinism: at any instant it's in exactly one state; if you don't know which, that's your ignorance, not the bit's condition. Exclusivity: one bit holds one value at a time, never a combination. And non-disturbing readout: you can read or copy a bit without changing the original.

One bit has 2 possible states, two bits have 4, and in general n classical bits have 2 to the n possible configurations — that's why 8 bits give you 256 values and 32 bits can address over four billion locations. But that exponential counts the size of the space the system could occupy, not how many it's in at once. At any given moment, an n-bit register holds exactly one of those strings, like 01101010, and nothing else.

That's what makes classical bits a strictly weaker model: they only ever occupy pure, definite, mutually exclusive states, and any uncertainty is purely about an observer's incomplete knowledge. There's no mechanism for a single physical system to carry structured information about several possibilities at once in a way that can later interfere. That absence is the entire reason quantum computing is a separate field, not just faster transistors.
Next lesson introduces the real object quantum mechanics permits in place of the classical bit: the qubit, formally defined as a state vector, not a bit that's secretly both 0 and 1 at the same time.
